utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Buenos dias. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gracias, gracias. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Sarapa, who was supposed to give us an answer today. He's still thinking about it. Mr. Bourgon is also not present, and Mr. Meek. The Prosecution team is as was yesterday; that's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. The witness is present in the courtroom. Good morning to you, Colonel. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with the examination-in-chief, and then we'll see what happens after.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, you were speaking about the men boarding the buses in fear. You mentioned that you saw that they had to discard all of their belongings. Do you recall whether or not that included identification? And forgive me if I asked you this.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they left everything that they had. That included their identification cards, the money that they had in their pockets, that is, their wallets and whatever was inside there, and also they had luggage that they were carrying that maybe included clothing and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you recognised at least one person with whom you'd become familiar from your time in Srebrenica town. Colonel, when these men were being placed on these buses, were you able to make any effort to record their identities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did. I tried to record whatever I could get concerning the identities, and at one point I could tell them to shout their names to me so that I could write them as they were leaving, heading towards the buses, but that failed because some of the names I could not be able to write them properly, even when they shouted. But that was my attempt to make sure that at least those who were going in, there's someone who knows who they are. But I did not finish that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 512 on e-court, please. To move things along, we can see this is a daily sitrep from UNMO headquarters in Tuzla to BH Command UNMO in Sarajevo and Zagreb, and this is for the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 4 of the English, and that will be page 5 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's focus on paragraph 1 for a moment, Colonel, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference, second sentence: UNMO's assessed that there are about 10.000 people inside and 20.000 people outside. When this report states there are 10.000 people inside the compound, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this meant was that the number of refugees, if we can use that word, because they were not in their normal places of dwelling, inside the Dutch-Bat compound, inside the main hall, there were about 5.000 or slightly over 5.000, and those who were around and within that general compound could have been around 4.000 to 5.000. That is why the figure, to us, came to about 10.000. And for your information, the way we arrived at these figures is the way these people were huddled together inside, in that you could see a group of around 50, 60. Then you could calculate the groups and then come to a round figure that can guide you, because we did not do the physical checks, but according to the way we -- way we analysed the whole situation, the number of people inside there were about 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A little further down, paragraph 2, Colonel, there is a reference to patients numbering more than 80. Do you know where these 80 patients were coming from, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of these patients were referred to Dutch-Bat compound because there was a hospital there by the MSF. Others just brought themselves and they fell sick, some were sick, others were injured, and that is how we got the identity of them inside the Dutch-Bat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened to the patients being treated in the hospital in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Srebrenica town, the treatment was -- they had only one doctor, and the treatment could not have been that -- it had its own limits, in that they did not have a proper surgical ward, and the people to help, and that is the nurses, were not that many. So the treatment was not as good or as advanced as it was in Dutch-Bat compound because of the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall whether or not the patients who were being treated in the Srebrenica Hospital during the course of the attack were ever moved out of the hospital at any time; and if so, where were they moved?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were. They were moved to the Dutch-Bat compound, and in fact the last patients, I was in that team that brought them over to Dutch-Bat hospital from Srebrenica Hospital. Also, there are some that were taken direct to Bratunac Hospital, together with some others who were in the Dutch-Bat compound, but that was much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many patients were transferred from the Srebrenica Hospital to the Dutch-Bat compound, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot recall the actual figure, only that the last ones, there were about six. The last ones to be transferred were six, and I was involved. I personally was there to get them out of Srebrenica Hospital to Dutch-Bat compound, and I think that that was the last group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could look at the very bottom of the page in English, and that's going to be the bottom of page 6 in the B/C/S version, there's a reference to: "We had to dismantle the station as the BSA trooped into the streets of Potocari and further spreading to take positions all around the near vicinity of the Dutch-Bat compound." What is this station that this person is referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This station was our communication station, that is, the UNMOs. Hours after we entered the Dutch-Bat compound, we established it in -- in a container outside the main -- the main building. And when these just came all over the place, we feared they might either take our communication equipment or interfere with communication, so we had to dismantle and take them inside the main -- the main building where Dutch-Bat were, where we thought maybe slightly more secure, because outside in the container, it definitely was not as secure as inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, given the level of activities that you've testified you were engaged in over these last couple of days, who was it that was spending most of the time manning that communications station?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would alternate between the three of us, that is, myself, Major Tetteh and Major Andre De Haan. We would alternate. Sometimes we could have me being there and then the others outside. One could be at the -- with the refugees in the main -- in the main hall, the other one outside the compound. That is where they were grouped, in the outside compound, and along the streets. So we were spread thinly all over, and one could be manning their station at one time or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's talk about July 13th, Colonel. Did you have occasion to investigate any particular locations in Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on July the 13th, there was a report from some Dutch-Bat soldiers that there were some civilians who were being taken -- some BiH civilians that were being taken -- that is, Muslims that were being behind a certain building, and whenever they were taken behind there, they never returned. And in the process, there could be heard some shooting, and that shooting was a bit -- it was single-round shots; that is, upon further investigation, that is what we were told. So I decided to go -- to go behind there to go and check, and when I -- I tried my first attempt, I was told by the BSA soldiers who were there that I cannot go through, that I should not go in there. So I went back, but I later insisted and tried to go in. I managed to go slightly further, and I saw some soldiers -- some Muslim men being taken -- I think one of them was being taken behind there. I witnessed that. And they prevented me from going further, and they even told me that if I tried to go further than that, they were going to shoot me. So I had no choice other than to turn back. And for your information, I heard a shot as I went back, so I did not stay there long enough to see whether that person came out or not, but for sure, I heard a gunshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, using the building in which you saw the Muslim men being crowded as a point of reference, can you describe the approximate location of where this place that you've just been describing was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the building was not very far from the -- the vicinity of the Dutch-Bat compound. It was slightly towards -- as you head towards Srebrenica village from Potocari, and somewhere -- somewhere in between Dutch-Bat compound and where these -- the civilians were herded outside, that is, the Muslims, where they were outside a factory there, it was somewhere -- somewhere there. I can't recall the exact location, but it's somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you leave Potocari at some point on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I left Potocari the 13th. I really can't remember. I can't remember very well, but -- I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall going to Srebrenica at some point during these couple of days after the transportation of the civilian population began?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do. I do remember one time we -- there's a time that we went to pick those injured with an MSF lady, and in the process we -- we saw what had been told to us, that the Bravo Company compound had been shelled, and we saw -- I actually saw the crater, that is, you know, where the place had been shelled, and we passed through, although you could see -- you could not -- I could not have time to analyse the crater, but at least I could see some blood spilled all over. And then we went to Srebrenica itself. I think this is the time that either we picked the sick or -- there was a lady who was -- who had refused to leave that -- that place, and we persuaded, but I think this is the last time that we went to pick the last sick people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, and let me ask you a couple more questions about that occasion. On the way to Srebrenica, was there anything that you recall standing out in your mind about that trip to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you describe again, what exactly was the purpose, as best as you can recall, for this trip to Srebrenica? Why were you being asked to go there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two issues here that are conflicting in my mind. One of them was that of the -- these sick -- sick people who were left in the hospital, and the other one is about a meeting that we were to hold, called by Colonel Karremans, I think, to talk to the BiH. And I can't remember which one it was, but I think there was a meeting called by Colonel Karremans with the Muslim leaders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you did when you arrived at the hospital in Srebrenica that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I arrived at the hospital, the first thing I noticed was that the whole place really was -- was in a mess, and the -- the sick, actually, there was no one who was taking proper care of them. And the soldiers, the BSA soldiers, were all over. In fact, they were looting. They were looting everything they could -- they could get. And the sick, you know, they themselves did not know what would happen to them, and in fact they did not care because they were -- they were old and they seemed not to know what was happening or what should be done about the whole situation. But the soldiers there were insistent. You know, they wanted these people to be removed from the hospital, we go with them, or they -- in their own words, they said, if you don't go with them, they are going to shoot them, they are going to kill them. So that was a bit -- a bit hostile, but that is what they said. So we had to go with them. Otherwise, they could have eliminated them. I think that is what is most outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you return to Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Major Nikolic in Potocari on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Nikolic came in to verify the -- mainly to verify the list of the people who were in the Dutch-Bat compound with the one that he had. His main reason was to check whether there were any Muslim soldiers inside there, and also if they were there, you know, how did they get in there, were they armed and did they have -- if they were injured, what kind of injuries and where were they injured, all those things. That is what we wanted to check, at least to confirm whether they are soldiers and what they are doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not Major Nikolic was alone during this process?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember very well Major Nikolic was not alone. He was with Colonel Vukovic and Colonel Drcic [Realtime transcript read in error "Andric"]. And there were some others, but at least those I remember very well were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 514, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check whether "Colonel Andric" is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Your Honour. I just noticed that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript indicates that you stated that Major Nikolic was with Colonel Vukovic and Colonel Andric. Is that correct or -- or not, "Andric"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct, it's Colonel Drcic. I can spell if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, to the best of your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the spelling was Delta-Romeo-India-Charlie-India-Sierra [sic]. I think that's the spelling, "Drcic."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is a sitrep update --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment here. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have not noticed this on the list of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is on the list. It's also been marked as 488. It was marked twice. I think we indicated that on our list as well. You'll see if you go to 488, it's also listed as 514. One of those situations where it gets multiple numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we're looking at a sitrep update at 0800 on the 13th of July. I just want to turn your attention to two things. At the very bottom of this report, it states: "We tried to investigate the rumour that the Serbs should have killed several men they took out of the crowd yesterday." What is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what I have alluded to you earlier, that there were men who were being taken from the group and taken behind a white building somewhere by there, and most of the time they -- I mean, in fact, they never returned, so this is the people he's -- we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The sign-off line reads: "TA team, TL." You've already told us what "TA" means. What does "TL" stands for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "TL" stands for "Team Leader," and in this case this was Andre De Haan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 515, and this has also been marked as 489.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I just want to draw your attention to the "To" and"From" line. We have a date here of 13th of July, 1100 hours, sitrep update. The "From" is "TA," the "To" is "TX." What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To," that is, "TX," stands for another team. I can't remember whose team that was, but it was the code name for another team. And of course "Tango Alpha," you know, it was Team Srebrenica. So in this case, it used to happen that sometimes you're sending the sitrep to your headquarters, and due to communication problems, it does not reach. You may even try a second time and it does not go through, so you may opt to transmit through another team site who maybe will be able to re-transmit the same to your headquarters. That is what used to happen in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Turning your attention to paragraph 4, in particular paragraph 4(a), which reads: "The number of departed refugees is about 10.000 by now." Do you recall how that figure was arrived at?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was in accordance with -- with the number of buses that had departed. We were calculating the capacities of the buses and their number, and then we calculated and found that the figure was around 10.000 people who had departed by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, just a couple of other questions. If we go down to paragraph 6, and this will be on both versions, we'll be looking at paragraphs 6 and 7. Paragraph 6 refers to 50 babies being delivered, one woman dying and being buried on the compound, and another woman and a baby dying on a convoy to Tuzla. Do you have any personal recollection of any of these events, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At least I know about the 50 babies being delivered inside there, in that even the ones who were assisting were mainly the Dutch-Bat women who were assisting in these deliveries. Others were being done by the normal -- by the Muslims themselves. And I was witness to some of this, but at least I could see the kids immediately thereafter. Now, for the woman who died, she died inside the compound, inside there, and we were -- we were there. And she was taken out and buried. I think she was buried behind -- behind the factory. I cannot recall very well, but she was buried there. At least I know about that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just follow up with one question on that, Colonel. Is it your recollection that she was buried within the confines of the Dutch-Bat compound or somewhere outside the confines of the Dutch-Bat compound, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was behind the factory, but I cannot recall very clearly whether it was inside the compound or just slightly outside. That, I'm not very sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to "factory," you're referring to the main building on the Dutch-Bat compound that was formally a battery factory; is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, that is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the woman and a baby who died, this was communicated to us by the escort group, the Dutch-Bat guys who escorted these refugees out of Srebrenica, so they're the ones who told us about the death of one woman and a baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the next paragraph, number 7, it reports that Colonel Acamovic is the special representative of General Mladic who -- I presume that reads "is taking care of the operation from now on." Who was Colonel Acamovic, sir? Did you meet him? Do you know what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is someone I had met before, and he was present in most of the occasions, and he introduced himself as someone who was being appointed by General Mladic to take over all the operations inside the enclave now from General Mladic. He was like a special representative of the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if any, activities in particular you observed this Colonel Acamovic being involved in during this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the whole evacuation process was done in his -- in his presence, and also these other side issues, like that of taking some -- some men behind the building and shot or killed, all that was happening in his reign, and also the whole process until we left the enclave, all the way until the end of our journey from the enclave, I think he was the one in charge. So there were so many things which happened. Some of those are the ones I've told you, and also even the -- the separation of the men from the women, obviously he was -- he was still there, he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 516, please. We're looking at what's headed as a sitrep update and "answer to your questions," 1715 hours on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just drawing your attention to paragraph 2(c), where it states that: "Colonel Acamovic is the logistics officer of the staff of General Mladic. He looks like a reasonable person, in the age of about 50 years old. The talks with him were very friendly and understanding. Sorry we don't have more on him." Do you know what the source of this information was, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I talked to -- I remember talking to a guy who introduced himself as the -- as the legal officer, and he's the one who told me that Colonel Acamovic is actually a logistics officer in the staff headquarters of General Mladic. Also -- we were getting this information also from the normal people that we were dealing with, that is, Major Nikolic and Mr. Petar. At least there were several sources of getting this information. So for sure we had reason to believe that he was a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's look at 65 ter 517, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Looking at a sitrep update. The date is the 13th of July, 2045 hours. Just turning your attention to paragraph 1, where it states: "All the refugees are on the move now. Also the compound is abandoned from refugees." Two sentences later, it reports that an UNMO patrol escorted MSF to rescue six more old sick women from the hospital and psychiatric clinic in Srebrenica town. What is this referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is referring to the actual situation on the ground at that particular moment, in that in the Dutch-Bat compound, they only have 59 who were -- who were left, that is, the patients, and they were just waiting for transport to -- to go, and these -- look at it from a scenario whereby you had around 10.000 people who were inside and then you were left with only 59, so it was quite a big change. Now, the other sick -- the six who were in the psychiatric ward in the Srebrenica Hospital are the ones we went to pick with the MSF team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving down this document, sir, do you see where paragraph 2 begins?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It reads: "The UNHCR convoy came in as the last refugees went out (what an expert timing)." What is this referring to, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is referring to, I think, the fact that the UNHCR convoy is supposed to have come earlier to come and serve the people who -- who were in there, but somehow it just came in when the last refugees were leaving. So it's a bit -- looks a bit cynical, but what it means is that that timing, why could it have -- why couldn't it have been better? Why couldn't they have come slightly earlier so that at least they can assist the refugees before they leave, because essentially that is what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving a little further into the paragraph, Colonel, it describes the condition of the compound, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Beginning at paragraph 3, it reads: "Tears were in our eyes when seeing the desperate displaced persons with no secure future, looking at us and seeking for help we cannot give them. We really lost this enclave and our heads. We feel very sad that we were not able to do more. Only regards remain in this situation." Colonel, who wrote these words; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, of course anything written by the team is us, we are the ones who wrote, but these particular words were written by Major De Haan, but actually it's us as a team. What this explains is the actual feeling that we had inside there at that particular moment, in that you see the displaced people, people who you've come here to ensure their security is guaranteed, people you had stayed with for about three months or so, people who thought you were the only source of their security and safety, people who thought that you could be heard in the process of ensuring that they are secure, but now they have been left alone, on their own. They have been left to be harassed by the BSA, to be removed from where they claimed was their place. As far as they knew, that was their place. So you could see the way these people were feeling and the way on our side, also, as people who were entrusted in the safety and security of these people, being unable to ensure it, due to various reasons, and the desperation was everywhere. Even on our own side, we were desperate. We were thinking, why did we fail, why were we unable to contain this situation? Your Honour, when I say "we," in fact we're also referring to the whole UN system, so why, how come we could not ensure the security and safety of this enclave which was actually called "a safe area"? So that feeling and the realisation that this is actually the end, because the last people are about to leave the enclave, really could have, you know, driven someone to write such things. In fact, we were a bit -- he was -- we were a bit diplomatic, we were trying to be a bit diplomatic, but let me tell you for sure: If you are in a similar situation, it's -- it's okay now that we are not in the same situation, but, Your Honour, this was a very sad moment. This was a very sad moment for all of us in that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, that brings us to the 14th of July, Colonel. The civilian population has been moved out. Who remained, other than Dutch-Bat and UNPROFOR staff and employees?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the wounded also remained behind, the wounded, together with us and the -- the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the issues or concerns were that occupied you over the next few days after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, one of the major issues was our final evacuation from the -- from the enclave; that is, we, as the UNPROFOR, that is, the Dutch-Bat and us, and also the -- the sick, the injured, were with us, and the civilian employees. So we were very concerned about how we will exit that place, how safe will it be. Also, we were being told by the -- our headquarters that we should persuade the BSA to let us continue staying there to observe the situation in that area, and there was a lot of resistance from the BSA side in allowing us to continue, because their headquarters was insisting that we should remain as observers there, there should be a post, that we should remain there, so we tried to persuade them and they said, no, they cannot allow. And especially when it became apparent that if an UNMO team would be left there, maybe ours would have to be rotated, they feel they cannot have another team which they do not know. So those were our major -- our major concerns at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 519, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're looking at a sitrep update, 14 July, 1420 hours. I'd like to focus your attention on paragraph 5, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some questions about some of the wounded or injured or sick that are described in the second half of this paragraph, which begins with: "Because of the delay, one of the patients suffering from diabetes is in a very bad condition now." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a description of two patients who died, another patient who the doctors think may die, and one wounded Muslim soldier who attempted to hang himself. Do you have any personal recollection of any of these patients, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Your Honour, these -- these sick people who were inside there became our main concern, and some were because they were the most critical. We were looking at them as our major -- our major concern, so when their condition, especially of these -- these two started deteriorating, we were all involved, the doctors, we as observers, the, you know, Dutch-Bat team also. We were all getting concerned, and the death of, I think, these two also, you know -- we could not believe because we thought these are people who can be saved. But unfortunately, they could not be saved at all. Then the diabetic one, that one, we had no proper treatment for -- for him, and in fact we were -- we wanted him to be transferred to Bratunac Hospital because we had no proper treatment for him. We were just -- the doctors were just trying to keep him on for a while, but, you know -- and we were hoping always that he is going to -- to remain, he's not going to die. Now, on the -- on the one who tried to hang himself, this is someone that I actually met after he was saved by the Dutch-Bat people. He was -- he was actually just about to kill himself, and he felt, now that the enclave was being taken over, he would be found by Major Nikolic and he would definitely be killed. Not by him; I mean he would definitely be taken over. And he thought the best thing was to kill himself. He attempted, but luckily or otherwise, he failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not he had already been identified by Major Nikolic at the time he made the decision to try to take his own life?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he had been identified by Major Nikolic as one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 7. It reports that: "We also hear some shooting from the area of Bratunac. We again can investigate what is going on over there. Because the men were taken in separate buses, we fear for the worse." Again, "ROM." What does that refer to again, "ROM"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, "ROM" stands for "Restriction of movement." The other side of it is the freedom of movement, which is the "FOM." So in this case, what we are trying to say is that in Potocari, we could hear shooting coming from the direction of Bratunac, at least we can be able to know the direction, because Bratunac was not too far from Potocari, so we could -- we could know it was coming from there. And because the men had been taken towards that direction, you know, it occurred to our minds that maybe something is happening to them, maybe something wrong, maybe some shooting, maybe they are being killed, but we could not be able to confirm this because we could not move to that area. It was our duty to go and investigate, to go and see what is happening, but we had a restriction of movement, and, as such, we could not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the shooting that you did hear?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- it's a bit difficult to describe it, in that some, you could hear single shots, you could hear single shots, and at other times you could hear a burst. But most of the time, it was -- it was a single shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 521, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we're looking at an UNMO, headquarters Tuzla, daily sitrep for the 15th of July. If we could turn to page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S, please. And we'll be focusing on paragraph (c). Do you see the section that reports that the BSA have confirmed that they are holding a quantity of males in Bratunac and Srebrenica, they have declared that the civilian males will be released soon and the ABiH males will be held for the purpose of POWs." Do you recall seeing that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving this information, and if you do, who did you receive it from?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this information came in two -- came in twofold. That is, first and foremost, I was told by the -- by the legal officer or the officer who introduced himself as the legal officer that the reason -- you know, when I asked him why they were holding men separately from the women, he told me that they were doing that so that men can be transported separately. Later on, when I insisted, he said they are taking the men separately so that if they find there's some soldiers therein, they would -- they would be able to exchange them with their own prisoners of war who were held by the other side, that is, by the Muslims. So he told me that exactly the main reason why they are holding them. And for sure, to them -- to him it made sense, in that if they have men they can hold as prisoners of war and the others have theirs, they can just swap over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as to this particular report on this day, sir, do you recall from whom this information came?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure, I can't tell where -- where it came from, but these must have come maybe from us. I'm not very sure, but it is possible, but I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't mean who was the source of the information to Tuzla. I mean, other than this legal officer, who you've described before, you said first and foremost you were told by this legal officer at some other point, my question is: On the 15th of July, as reflected in this report, Colonel, do you have any recollection of what the source of this particular report was to you or your UNMO team?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've -- you've already referred to efforts to transport some wounded and injured from Potocari to the hospital in Bratunac. Do you recall who was involved on the Serb or civilian or VRS side with that effort?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- the Serb side, I think we had Major Nikolic, and also there was a civilian -- I think Civilian Affairs officer who was involved, but I cannot remember his name very well. But there was a Civilian Affairs officer and also Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, let's just look at a couple more documents. 65 ter 524, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're looking at a sitrep update, 2300 hours on the 17th of July, from Team Srebrenica to TX, which you described as another UNMO team. I want to focus your attention, sir, on paragraph 2, which is on page 1 of both versions. It refers to a meeting -- actually, a second meeting in which UNMO's DCO Dutch-Bat, Colonel Drcic, MSF and ICRC took part. What, if anything, do you know about this meeting, and do you recall who Colonel Drcic was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this meeting was organised by the deputy commanding officer of Dutch-Bat so that we could talk to the BSA side and agree on how we were going to handle the -- the injured, the sick who were in the Dutch-Bat compound. Our feeling was that they could be better handled in Bratunac Hospital, so we wanted to discuss it with them so that -- with them so that they can allow the transfer of these wounded to that hospital. And the Colonel Drcic was a senior officer there, and we had met on, I think, two or three other occasions, but I really cannot recall what his assignment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the Colonel Drcic to whom you referred earlier in your testimony and tried to spell his name?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, this is the same guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's a reference further into the paragraph that a Professor Koljevic had to be called. Do you know who Professor Koljevic was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall who he was. I know I met him -- I know he had to be called because we were told now we were looking for Colonel Koljevic -- Professor Kuljecic, but I really do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear for the record, is it your recollection that you have ever met him, and do you have any recollection of who he is or what his role was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic, I don't remember ever meeting him, and I do not know his role. It's only that we were told he had to be informed, he had to be called about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 3, it refers to: "The UNMOs also had a private meeting with Colonel Drcic about the issue of the team being able to stay in Bratunac with the full freedom of movement and guarantee of their safety and security. The colonel stated that as far as he was concerned, it would not be any problem because he had heard very good stories about us from Major Nikolic. Of course, he has to bring this subject up to his higher command." And if we go to page 2 of the English and the B/C/S, paragraph 4 picks up on a separate issue: "The Dutch-Bat rotation will be discussed tomorrow after Colonel Drcic has orders from his higher command." Do you recall this private meeting with Colonel Drcic, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do, and the main aim was twofold also, in that one was, like I had said earlier, that the -- the request by our headquarters was that an UNMO team -- UNMO presence be there in the enclave, and we were to request them whether they can give us the freedom of movement that is required of military observers so that we can do our job, which he failed to provide until confirming with higher authorities. Also, Dutch-Bat, they also request that it be rotated, so the Dutch-Bat, you know, go out and then another team comes in, maybe from the same country, but another team to come in, another battalion to come in. And this, he said, he could not -- he could not confirm until he gets instructions from above after he requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, these two references to Colonel Drcic's higher command, to your recollection, what level was his higher command, what level are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, "higher command," in this sense, you know, being a colonel, a higher command could have been the division, the division level, or even at the army level, that is, the headquarters level. So it could be -- it could be somewhere there, because as a full colonel, that is a -- he's of a senior rank. So we're talking about the division or the -- the army level.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One last document, sir. If we could look at 65 ter 526.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is a sitrep update, 1500 hours on the 18th of July. Paragraph 1 refers to a meeting at 1330 hours that the UNMO team had with the commanding officer of Dutch-Bat, Colonel Drcic, Major Nikolic, and Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, referring to as the Civil Affairs Commissioner for Srebrenica of the BSA. You referred to a civilian individual, sir, civilian authority individual earlier in your testimony. Does this refresh your recollection as to who that person was or are we talking about somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does, it really does. Now I can remember him, this Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. He was the Civil Affairs officer. I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything in particular about this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this meeting was to discuss the issues that I have just said earlier, and especially to do with Dutch-Bat, in that there was a need to rotate the Dutch-Bat, and this had to be discussed with the BSA. But Colonel -- Colonel Drcic was very clear that there was a meeting -- already a scheduled meeting between General Smith and General Ratko Mladic, and he said that these are -- they are going to discuss this, amongst many other issues. And I remember there's maybe a time that I talked about such a meeting, in that General Smith were to meet with General Ratko Mladic, you know, on -- at that level, they are to discuss on issues that mainly were big in nature, so there's nothing we could do at that time. We had to wait until we could hear the outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- when did you withdraw from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember very well, but I think it was on 20th, I think -- I think 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you withdraw with the rest of the Dutch forces or separately from them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surprisingly, we were -- we were there as military observers, unarmed, and we were told we were the ones to provide security to the -- to the Dutch-Bat, so we had to withdraw together. And on that day, I remember we talked to Major Nikolic, and he told us that it was all safe, because they are the ones to ensure that we were -- we had a safe passage out of the enclave. And as we embarked on the -- on the way out, we were told that General Mladic would be somewhere on the way to say goodbye to us. So we escorted Dutch-Bat out. We had one patrol in front and another one behind, and we escorted them out of the enclave, together with ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I want to do with you last is show you a few video clips, short clips, and a photograph first. If we could look at 65 ter 448, please. Do you see the image in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt, this is Petar, our BSA interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you some brief video clips. We are beginning at one hour 58 minutes and 8.3 seconds of a clip V000-4417.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you just viewed this brief clip that has ended at one hour 58 minutes 24.3 seconds. Did you recognise yourself in that clip at any time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, I could see someone who looks like me. I think I'm the one. But he looks a bit younger than me now, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we're pausing here, and do you see three dogs in this frame?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see them. These are big -- huge dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the presence of dogs with the BSA soldiers on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. I object to that line of questioning. I believe that my colleague should have asked the witness, before he showed this video clip, if he remembered seeing any dogs in Potocari, but not after showing him this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have no problem with proceeding this way, although maybe technically you are correct. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall whether or not there were dogs being handled by Serb forces during the 12th and the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the dogs were there. I saw them, I personally saw the dogs, and they were huge, huge dogs, which like the ones I know in Nairobi, this size, these are the ones which are trained, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's resume, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we're at one hour 58 minutes 33.3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see anybody you recognise? Do you see yourself, let me just put it that way, in this video, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I can recognise General Ratko Mladic who is to the -- to the right. Your Honour, I can recognise him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's resume, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier, by the way, the soldier who is in blue, this is not a UN soldier. This is not a UN soldier, but he has a blue helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You don't recall this individual as being a UN soldier, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, you're in the sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in sunglasses which somewhere sometimes someone wanted to snatch them from me, but he was requested to give them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's look at the second clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, that clip began at two hours 25 minutes 39 seconds. We paused at two hours 28 minutes 45.4 seconds. What are you referring to here, where we've paused? You're addressing someone, some people. I want to ask you what you were referring to, and who were you addressing, and why?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue at hand at this particular moment was the men who were overcrowded in one -- in one building. There were too many of them. There was no -- no water, no sanitation. There was no food for them, and there didn't seem to be any air, because they were overcrowded, and at least seen from some distance and I could see the condition they were in. So I was trying to talk to anyone who at least could understand what I'm talking about and someone who could speak a bit of English, because there were very few Serbs who could -- who could speak English at that particular moment. And one of the soldiers behind there, the one I was talking to, he was maybe somehow to my left, could speak English, and that is a guy I wanted to convey the same to the senior -- to the senior officers. If possible, we go -- in fact, the aim was we go with him to the senior officers so that he can explain the situation that is actually of major concern to me at that particular moment, and that is why I was talking to him. And the issue at hand was the general condition of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if anything in particular, this person you were using as an interpreter was wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular man was wearing a blue -- a blue UN -- a blue vest, that is, a bulletproof vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep rolling the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, pausing at two hours 29 minutes 57.5 seconds, do you recall where this location is depicted in this still?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is on the main road towards Bratunac, that is, outside the Dutch-Bat compound, and as can be depicted from this -- this picture is that I was discussing with these -- with this person so that he can convey this same message, after translating it, to the senior officers there, because at least he could speak a bit of -- a bit of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, when you're referring to the interpreter, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I'm referring to this person who is in a blue UN vest and who is in the picture to my -- to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the individual who is next to this individual, between you and this individual you've described in the blue vest, do you recognise this individual at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this was a senior officer in the BSA. Right now I cannot remember his -- his name properly, but he was one of the senior officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let's roll the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've paused at two hours 30 minutes 46.6 seconds. Do you recall what's depicted in this frame?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the house we were talking about, the one I said earlier, where all the men were -- were herded into. This is the place that, after the men were separated from the women, were all taken to. You can even see the -- the overcrowding that I was talking about. There seems to be no space at all in between the individuals. They are in a terrible state inside there, and this is just one part, one of -- I think this is the first floor or something. Below, it was the same, and it was quite a mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. We'll have a break now, 25 minutes, and then we'll see how we are going to proceed. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the way, the usual lapses. This is to confirm that we have been sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today from the beginning because of the inevitable absence of Judge Stole. Yes, Colonel. What was your rank at the time in 1995, when you were living these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in 1995 I was the rank of a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A major. Okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you prepared to go ahead with your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, but I'd prefer to take my stand after recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why? You think you will feel more energetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will conduct a better cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's one of the reasons for that. And as I understand my friend yesterday, he has to disclose some additional documents and to provide Rule 70 clearance, and to have a proofing with the witness regarding these documents, so I'd like to start my cross-examination after that. But I'm ready if you order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see you have quite a voluminous file in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's think about it. In the meantime, we'll do what we promised to do yesterday. Colonel, for the time being, I think we need to stop here. I will soon send you a message, whether your presence is further required for the rest of the morning. The understanding is that you will be returning in January. I'm hoping you won't be sent back to Kenya when we need you. And if we don't see each other again today, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, we wish you not only a safe journey back home, and also a return back to The Hague, a safe journey, but we also wish you all the very best for the festive season.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a pending motion, Prosecution motion, for the addition of one witness. I don't -- I needn't mention his name. And we discussed the possibility of having this determined now, before the break, before the recess, so that everyone will be in a position to know what's going to happen. I asked Mr. Sarapa yesterday also because this witness is of more interest to your client than to anyone else, and he obviously needed to consult with you and also with the other Defence teams. What's your position? Are you in a position to give us your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I've read and considered the motion, and I can't see any sensible opposition to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Does anyone else from the Defence teams oppose the motion? So step number 1, we are granting the motion. We don't need to follow it up with a written decision. I suppose you can work out the necessary applications for visa without a written decision; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And the understanding is that you try and see when you will fit him within the schedule and that you inform the Defence teams, particularly the Pandurevic Defence team, as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, this witness will be referred to as "Witness number 192."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness number 192, okay. But it's not my understanding that you're seeking protective measures for him; are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We frankly don't know yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, thank you. There is another -- let me bring it up here. Yesterday evening, the Prosecution filed a further motion to add two witnesses to its 65 ter list, these being an ICMP employee who will testify about the methodology of the DNA identification process, and Ms. Ewa Tabeau, who will testify on the process of updating the list of Srebrenica missing persons. Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We do object to the motion filed in connection with the ICMP and Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First of all, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it because you didn't question the witness on precisely the same matters that the Prosecution seeks to clarify now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not because of that, Your Honour. First, I think that the Court has set certain guidelines for identifying witnesses, and I think that given how late we are in the stage of the proceedings and with one month left for the Prosecution to conclude their case in chief, I think quite candidly, it's very untimely to bring in witnesses. With respect to the ICMP witness, we were not given any information whatsoever as to who the individual is or the basis of the testimony that they will be providing. Secondly, with respect to Ms. Ewa Tabeau, she is an in-house demographer that has assisted Mr. Brunborg. And her reports, I think it's just going to be cumulative from what Mr. Brunborg has already testified to and given his reports. We think that the Prosecution, with all due respect to them, wanted to have Ms. Tabeau, they should have listed her earlier and they should have identified her months ago, when she was compiling this data. We also disagree with the Prosecution that it would be unfair to the Defence. We think that that's just their standard statement to meet some threshold. They don't give a basis, we think, because of the late disclosure, the not -- non-sufficient disclosure of information from both witnesses, that the Court should reject their motion, they should not be permitted to add these witnesses to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Does anyone else wish to address the Chamber? Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Good morning. Good morning to my colleagues. I would just like to add some more things that I'm more concerned about in relation to the ICMP witness. What I did not manage to speak to my colleagues about is this: Are we speaking about an expert witness or a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't understand it at any time to be a proposal on the part of the Prosecution to bring an expert witness. I haven't understood it that way. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, perhaps you can deal with this first so that Ms. Nikolic can finish her intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't yet have the name of the person, so it's -- this person's level of expertise, I don't know. He may, in fact, or she may, in fact, be a chemist of some sort, but fundamentally, we're not calling the person for chemistry or biogenetics or whatever, but mostly just for the processes, not the science. As I said, I think, yesterday, I don't think there's a scientific objection about DNA, but the general processes, I think, is what this is about, and I will get into more detail in responding to Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes, Ms. Nikolic. Do you wish to conclude your intervention? No. Ms. Nikolic. I'll give you the floor soon, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that I cannot finish what I am saying until the Prosecution decides in the case that we have a witness who's only going to talk about the compilation of data, that's one thing. But as for the analysis, the reliability, percentages, the procedures and methods, this is something that the Defence would need to deal with, in particular, so I want to just leave this question open for now and I will try and see and speak to my colleagues to see exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, we tried to have a meeting this morning because the motion of the Prosecution yesterday was submitted quite late. According to what the Prosecutor said now, that they don't know what kind of witness they will have and what their specialty will be, whether it will be a chemist or some other kind of specialist, it's perfectly clear that the Prosecution absolutely cannot determine the field of expertise of this witness, what the witness will be talking about. If it's not an expert of the appropriate profile, then there is the possibility that the testimony of that person from the ICMP would be repetitive in relation to the testimony of witness Dean Manning, so that is why I believe that there are no conditions, there are no basic parameters from the Prosecution, in order for us to be able to decide whether to object to their proposal or not. So we object to including such a person on the list at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Tapuskovic. As I read paragraph 4 of the motion, what it says is: "The ICMP employee will testify about the methodology of the DNA identification process and confirm the accuracy and reliability of the underlying identification data used to prepare the lists of the Serbians who are missing, as well as to prepare the 27 November 2007 Dean Manning report." Does anyone else from the Defence team wish to address the Chamber, failing which I will give the floor to Mr. McCloskey? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and briefly I'll try to remind counsel how this has all arisen. I had not planned to call anybody from ICMP originally, nor did I plan to call Helge Brunborg again or his assistant here -- that works here, because when Helge Brunborg testified about this material and outlined the methods and procedures and his confidence in it as an expert in the field, no one objected, and therefore we didn't feel the need to go into it. It didn't appear anyone had any real concerns about the issues of getting bones from relatives of missing people and connecting their blood, which is a very -- it's pretty basic and easy to describe, though it's complex in the detail. Now, when Dean Manning was relying on the same -- much of the same data as Helge Brunborg, as you remember Ms. Soljan told us, we got an objection of the same material, and so at that point I -- I've spoken and I'm hearing myself speak again on the same subject, that if that's the case, if we're getting an objection, we relied on their non-objection before, so since they are objecting and they're calling into question this material, then we are offering to bring in the person from ICMP to meet their objection. And because the data comes in a raw form from ICMP, we need Ewa Tabeau to package it a bit for us so that it's -- so they'll understand how it got used in -- for Dean Manning and for Helge Brunborg. Should the Defence withdraw all those objections regarding DNA and they're willing to stand by it, I'd just as soon not get into this subject, but we're ready to do it. It's fascinating stuff and it's an important programme, and it's, unfortunately, a field that is growing. And with things like 9/11, it may be becoming an expertise, actually, what they are doing. But that's what this is about. That's why we're filing it at this time. It's in response to their objection, having not objected to the same material a few months back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further but to repeat that we object to all findings of Mr. Brunborg, but we didn't object to admissibility of his report because he testified here that he made this report and we have no grounds to object to in this regard. But all findings of Mr. Brunborg were objected by us from the very start, and I expected Mr. McCloskey to comply with the order of the Trial Chamber and file his motion about -- regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I absolutely agree with Mr. Zivanovic. That's not what I'm saying. But he -- there's a difference between objecting to the admissibility and objecting to the numbers. I, of course, know that he's been fighting the numbers all along, and I understand that, but he did not object to the admissibility, which is what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the whole crux of the matter, actually. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is, first of all, the understanding is that because of the urgency of the matter and the fact that we are going on recess and such decisions need to be taken with some urgency, we have dispensed with the usual time limits for the filing of responses, and I wish to thank you all for your cooperation in this. Our position is as follows: Prior to the testimony of Dean Manning and the raising of issues relating to the ICMP DNA fingerprinting analysis undertaking for establishing the identity of Srebrenica missing, and prior to that, our feeling, our conviction, is that the Prosecution is right in contending that there was no plausible reason for them to bring forward such evidence -- such additional evidence as is being sought now. The need for such evidence arose -- was prompted by the position taken by the Beara Defence team during their cross-examination and also by the statement forthcoming from the Popovic Defence team, which made things clearer than they might have been understood prior to then, so our first conclusion is we feel the need for such additional testimony, and we are granting the motion. However, there is one "but." A good point raised by Ms. Nikolic this morning is that the ICMP employee that will be produced as a witness here has not been identified, and also it is not clear, possibly even in your mind till now whether this individual, he or she, would testify merely on facts or whether as sort of an expert witness. So in granting the motion, we are also ordering the following or instructing you along the following lines: Number 1, you need to identify this person as soon as possible and decide in which vest you are going to produce this witness. The name of this person is to be communicated to the Defence teams in a pristine manner as early as possible and is to be accompanied by either a statement or a report, as it may be the case. And for that purpose, we are reserving for all the Defence teams any right -- residual right that they may still have to make submissions in relation to this would-be ICMP witness. In that case, please, we would expect you to make any further submissions on this matter once you have the details, possibly before we start again on the 10th of January. Is that clear? Okay. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't fully understand the objection. I take it there's not an objection as to the science of DNA matching. Because if that's the case, we have to add about six months on to our time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to take it from -- take the lead from the line of questioning that was taken by the Ostojic -- by the Beara Defence team during cross-examination. I think the contention at the time was that the ICMP report or findings, as such, were not being introduced as a separate expert report or a separate report from what Mr. Manning was providing us with, and I think from the questions asked to -- from Mr. -- put to Mr. Manning, you should have a clear answer, what is being contested and what is not. I think I would leave it at that. I wouldn't venture to add anything to it further. I think what's important is that the Dean Manning report makes reference to the ICMP findings, and I think we need to know something about -- about those, too. Now, let's come to the other issue. Yesterday I asked you, Mr. McCloskey, whether you were in a position to give your oral response to the Gvero Defence team motion relating to the testimony -- forthcoming testimony of Mr. Butler, and you said you would be in a position to give us your position today. So I don't think I need to come back to you first, Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, to explain the contents of your motion, because it's very clearly expressed, and I don't think it really calls for any further explanation. But of course you will have a right to respond after Mr. McCloskey has finished his intervention, if that is satisfactory to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is. I rather hoped that the Chamber aren't going to be troubled by this matter for too much longer, but we'll hear from Mr. McCloskey in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we had a bit of misunderstanding with the -- with the Defence. I was able to speak to Mr. Josse about this, and I think we've come to an agreement that we don't really have an issue anymore. And I'll give you the explanation. The material that I provided was never meant to be an additional report, and it was never -- the 109 documents that Mr. Butler reviewed was based on a process of material that he hadn't been able to review because he hadn't been here or we didn't have translations of, but that he either thought had something to do with his previous analysis or something that I thought had come up as an issue in the case that he should know about, and so we wanted to hear his comments on what turned out to be a final 109. I never intended to put 109 documents as exhibits before the Court in his testimony; maybe half of that. And I am continuing to -- to go down that list to try to restrict the exhibits. Mr. Butler is a person that if an exhibit, on its face, says what it says and everyone can read it, I don't want Mr. Butler to just repeat that to you. His value, as you've seen from the other motions, is linking that document or that fact with related facts in a complicated situation to help make sense out of it. And so in that case, I spoke to Mr. Josse, and the intercepts, for example, that he had a concern with. I'm not intending to ask Mr. Butler about those intercepts. They speak for themselves. One of the witnesses that was involved in them spoke to you. And there's three other documents that we spoke about that Mr. Josse doesn't have a problem with; Mr. Butler's brief connection. I spoke to Ms. Fauveau. There's several Miletic-type documents there, but Mr. Butler was just pulling them out of the convoy documents as -- to show that these were documents that showed restriction of convoy, and so -- and Ms. Fauveau didn't have a problem. So I don't think we have a problem. It's been restricted. We've had a chance to talk. It's not meant to be something that's changing anything or adding significance of the last detail. I'm very conscious of that as a problem and I don't want to do that. I've never wanted to do that. And I think once we've had a chance to talk about it, we shouldn't have a problem. And I don't know what you want to do with that, the proofing note, but I think it really is not something that I think we need to go any further on. And if there's any other help I can give anyone, let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put it like this -- let me hear what Mr. Josse has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we are very pleased to hear that and basically are prepared to withdraw the motion. I would like to state for the record that from the index of the 109 documents, the three documents that Mr. McCloskey has indicated he does wish to ask Mr. Butler about that are of relevance to our client are 68, 69 and 89, and we accept that he's going to do that and we have no objection to that. And on that basis, that is, that those are the only three documents of the 109 that relate to General Gvero that he's going to ask Mr. Butler about, we will withdraw the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, and that has the advantage of removing from our eyes the proofing note, which we would otherwise have to read for the purpose of deciding your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure all of us defending are glad about that, Your Honour. It was not an easy decision, to decide to annex it to the motion. We explained in the motion why we did that. Your Honour's aware that the Gvero team always take the view that the Chamber need to see the material before making a ruling, but since you don't need to make a ruling, as you've rightly observed, with respect, the document can be thrown away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. That sorts things out. One thing we also want to make clear, however, and this, too, is to avoid any further problems in anticipation of Mr. Butler's testimony, is that Mr. Butler is being produced as an expert in a particular field of expertise, and any questions to him should be confined to that field of expertise and not go beyond and invade other fields of expertise which he's not summoned to testify about. We are making it very clear, and it's being given to you as an advance notice. All right. That clears the territory, because there would have had -- there would have been problems arising out of the motion which would have involved other Defence teams, and they would have been perfectly justified in making submissions. We can leave it at that. The motion, for all intents and purposes being withdrawn, we will destroy our documents which we haven't read and -- I mean, we've read the motion, obviously, but pending the discussion on it, we haven't read any of the proofing notes or other accompanying material that there was with it. So shall we proceed with the cross-examination, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please convey to Colonel Kingori our decision not to proceed with his testimony for the rest of the day, and wish him all the best. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President. Excuse me, my cold is catching up with me finally. I just wanted to clarify one thing my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic mentioned. With respect to the Rule 70 documents that we hoped to hear from the New York headquarters about and the additional notebook and any reports, those we will -- with respect to specifically the notes, the notebook and the reports, we will handle all of that through the Witness Unit. Because he is still testifying, I will have no direct contact with him, obviously. I think my friend may have mentioned, maybe I misheard it, a future or an additional proofing session. I have absolutely no intention of proofing Colonel Kingori about any new information. It will simply be transmitted as we get it from the Victim/Witness Unit to my friends in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, is that clear in your mind, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I never understood that there was going to be a further proofing sessions between the Prosecution and Mr. Kingori prior to his return -- or after his returning to The Hague for the continuation of his testimony. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
