utterances.text: Just one other thing I'd spoken to my colleagues about, and I'm sorry I'm not more clear on the detail, but there's been some motions and there's some motions out there still, and there will be various deadlines that will be following in the next couple of weeks, and I think everyone has agreed to ask for a moratorium on responding. As Mr. Josse said so eloquently in his recent motion about this is the time not to work so much, I fully agree to that, and perhaps Ms. Fauveau would follow that for a change as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse is only half right, however, because even the Gvero team has in the past filed motions during the holiday or during recesses, and they're not the only ones. Even we have a standing team here throughout the entire recess period working on several issues, and we will be in contact with them on a daily basis ourselves so -- and possibly come down with some decision or decisions if we -- if they reach the maturity stage required. So, yes, the recess is supposed to be a time when we can recharge our batteries, but there is a lot of work still outstanding that needs to be attended to. However, before we rise ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I saw you standing, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we've got a few moments, I don't know whether now is the appropriate time for me to make a brief oral application in relation to the 98 bis procedure. It doesn't really need to be resolved now. We note, from the order that the Chamber issued, that the Chamber decided that the Defence had no right of reply. Speaking for myself -- we've had some discussion amongst the Defence teams about this, but speaking on behalf of my team only, we don't feel it's appropriate to ask the Chamber to tinker with the amount of time this has been allocated, but we wonder whether you would consider allowing us an hour and a quarter for our submission and reserving a quarter of an hour reply to whatever the Prosecution say. Replies, in our submission, are useful for the Chamber and important for the party responding, to have that opportunity to meet whatever's being said, both, frankly, as a matter of law and fact, but more a matter of law. It may be that an assertion of law is made and Defence neither accept it and, more to the point, say there is some alternative authority which the Court should examine. So the proposal, for want of a better word, that I'm making is that you allow a party, a Defence party, 15 minutes of their hour and a half for reply if they so choose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you speaking on your own behalf only or on behalf of the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm only speaking on my own behalf, because others perhaps might be a bit bolder and say they would like the right to reply and the hour and a half, but I'm not going that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think your decision was a sound one. I think the -- well, I know the burden of the proof is on the Prosecution, and should the Defence be given a reply in this context, the Prosecution should be able to reply to their reply. And so I think you've stopped it at the appropriate place, and I don't think we should go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only comment is the reply has to literally be a reply. It can't go beyond anything that has been said by the Prosecution in their response. So, in other words, it can't cover new material, and that is why, save in the most exceptional circumstances, there shouldn't be any call for what I think is called here a surreply. It simply shouldn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we need to discuss this any further for the time being. I think just mull over it, as Milton said, think about it, and re-digest it, and then if you think you wish to formulate it when we resume in January, that would still be a month before the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's very sensible, with respect. I simply mentioned it now because we had a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we -- we have a couple of exhibits for the Chamber that are the result of stipulations by the -- all the parties. They are two books that I've spoken of before. One is a book showing stills from the various trial videos showing mostly VRS or MUP, and then there's another book that show Muslims. We've had the finished product for you. The Defence has all theirs. There's been a stipulation. I think Ms. Stewart has the numbers, and I'm not sure it's in e-court yet. So we've got that for you, if you want it. We also, as -- we can deal with Dean Manning's exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to deal with those, but there are some further issues that I would like to deal with, but that's on the agenda, obviously. So one thing, this moratorium that you suggested, and you seem to be also echoing the desire or the wish of the Defence team, does it mean -- because we need to have things clear, in black and white, are you expecting or are you asking us to put in deep freeze all legal time limits applicable for possible responses and filings during the recess period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whatever I'm asking, I'm doing it with Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so, yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's hard to ask, and I can't really right now even figure out what's out there. But if there's anything out there that needs our response, we'll of course get it to you. But I don't think there's much that can afford not to be frozen, is my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is one very important issue, namely, the decision that we handed down recently on the intercepts, so if any of the parties, you or the Defence teams, wish to ask for certification, for example, are you proposing that the time limit fixed by the Rules for an application for certification will be suspended or put in freeze -- in deep freeze until the 10th of January or the 7th of January, when we are supposed to start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course we don't intend to file anything in relation to that, and I don't have an objection freezing that, perhaps. But whenever Mr. Bourgon is not in the courtroom, I'm always worried, so I'd like to freeze Mr. Bourgon for December. But that particular, I don't have any problem with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does any one of the Defence team wish to -- because our position, as far as the intercepts decision is concerned ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have raised the intercepts decision for an obvious reason; that according to our calculations, which I think are right, the due date for the filing of any application for certification is today. I don't know if any such filings have already been made, and I don't know if there is the intention of any one of the Defence teams to file such an application, but if it is filed, it's not our intention to then put in force or place in force a moratorium, giving you almost a month to respond to such application, Mr. McCloskey, and I'm pointing this out because you took it upon yourself to ask for a moratorium also on behalf of the Defence teams. The rest, I think, can be kept in deep freeze until January when we come back, but this one should be accepted, and we're making that clear. Okay? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey, the Dean Manning exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: We've just circulated to you a new list that contains only two additional documents to the list that was already circulated on Tuesday of this week, and I'll point out the additions. They are on page 2 of the exhibit list, under the dossier "Branjevo Military Farm." It's 3009, and it's an A3 aerial titled "Branjevo Farm," dated 17 July with markings by the provider. And it's page 6, right under expert reports, it's under 676, it would be 65 ter 3.010, and it's essentially just another report by Martin Ols. This has been actually added in agreement or per the request of the Nikolic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We continue to maintain our objection on the satellite images. If you'd like, I can read through these specific numbers, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need for that. I think your objection runs across all the satellite images that have been made use of by the Prosecution, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It does, Mr. President, and that would include the current one, 3009, from what I understand it, under the "Branjevo Farm" dossier section, but it does not include the one that she said there's a stipulation to. We also object, on page 6, to the ICMP data, both 3002 and 3004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Do you wish to comment on Mr. Ostojic's objection, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the ICMP data, Your Honours, this was the data on which Mr. Manning relied in order to produce his report. We would at least ask that it be marked for identification, pending the expert that we're expecting to get from the ICMP, who would then talk about it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Any objections, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I shouldn't have laughed. This has got nothing at all to do with General Gvero. I think the Court may know why I laughed, but others who are interested in the issue can perhaps pursue it better than I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence for Popovic, according to the list we have just received some 20 minutes ago from the Prosecution, although we are basing our submission on the list we received several days ago, wishes to ask for the admission into evidence of all the summaries of Witness Dean Manning, the 65 ter numbers 2993, 649, 648, 2994, 2994. I will give you a brief submission in relation to this. Where a piece of evidence is found to be relevant and of probative value, it has to pass the test of reliability. I believe that during the cross-examination by all the Defence teams of Witness Dean Manning, we arrived at the conclusion that the data he presented in his reports, particularly the November report, which is evidence 2993, that none of them passed the test of reliability. As far as the other evidence is concerned, we join with the Defence team for Beara, and we state the same reasons for our refusal to accept the ICMP documents. 3002 and 3004 are the numbers of the exhibits. This is the third batch of documents that was tendered for admission, and I believe that according to the list that you've just received in electronic form, it's also page 6, as is the case with the copy that I hold -- I'm holding in my hands that we received several days ago, and all the expert reports, 676, 675, 678, 562, 563 and 599. I'm referring to the decision rendered by the Trial Chamber shortly before the evidence of Dean Manning, 18096 is the transcript page, where you concluded that the witness would not be relying upon the expert evidence before the Trial Chamber, whereas during the examination-in-chief, the witness referred to the findings by other experts only in a sentence or two. That's why we oppose the admission of these documents into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. Ms. Soljan. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, I'm sorry, but there may have been a misinterpretation. At page 55, lines 23 and 24, it says "... Wishes to ask for the admission into evidence of all the summaries of Witness Dean Manning," and I'm assuming you meant -- or you may have said and it was misinterpreted, "oppose," I assume. That was the nature of your submission, but I just wanted to make sure I had that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that's correct. I wasn't able to follow the transcript as I was reading out the numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge Prost, and thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. I think the rest of the transcript makes it clear, because the reference is specifically to the four documents, four reports, Dean Manning reports, that the Prosecution was seeking to introduce. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe - excuse me - that there was just an objection to the fabric analysis and the report, as well as the report of Tony Brown on pollen analysis, and it was my understanding that we had a stipulation with the Defence that there was no objection to that, and that was one of the reasons why we reached some of the agreements that I have with the Defence. So I think perhaps that's a mistake on the part of the Popovic team or it's maybe they somehow got left out of those discussions. But if there is no -- if there is an objection to the -- to the fabric and pollen analysis, we're going to need to ask to call those witnesses, because this is totally against the understanding that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, with which we were not privy, of course. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There was extensive communication between the parties concerning the evidence of Mr. Manning, both before his evidence, during, and after. Now, whether Mr. McCloskey negotiated with some of the Defence teams the issue of the admission of expert findings, however, with us the possibility to stipulate some of the expert reports that I just referred to, well, I have to say that the Popovic Defence did not have any such contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, if I could try to clarify this for the umpteenth time. We're not asking them to stipulate to the findings of the report, just that they don't object to the admissibility. They object to the admissibility, they challenge the credibility of it, we're going to want to put on evidence. We had an agreement with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who took part in these discussions from the Popovic Defence team? I don't think -- I'm assuming that neither Mr. Zivanovic nor Ms. Tapuskovic were absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- I can tell you that my lack of objection to this 30-day extension to the 65 ter list was based on their agreement not to object to this scientific document. They are well aware of that, I know they are, and I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll cut this short. We'll ask you to file a motion, get these witnesses or get the necessary evidence, and if -- yes, if there has been a stipulation, there has been a stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could maybe have a short pause, a break, and then maybe we can just discuss this among ourselves and hopefully come to some resolution. I think there might be some miscommunication on that. A short five-minute recess, if the Court would indulge us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- may, I think, resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You for your wise suggestion, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think, as usual, the calming influence of Mr. Ostojic has brought us back on track, and I believe it's clearly understood that the Popovic team will, of course, be objecting to all that -- the substance of the material, but not the admissibility. And with that clear understanding, I think we're fine, and we can disregard anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Any further remarks? And I would have expected that, considering Mr. Ostojic's imposing stature compared to that of Mr. Zivanovic, so assuming that there has been no undue influence. Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to make one additional point about Mr. Manning's reports. The same thing; we are going -- we are now tendering them for admission. This is only an admissibility question. Obviously, we have a position on their reliability as well, given that they have been used and accepted into evidence in previous three trials, other than the newest to 1993, but we are tendering it into admission, and the weight will be up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, the weight is a matter reserved for the final exercise. All right. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic, do you wish to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Thank you, Your Honours. I thought it was my turn now for the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision on the Prosecution list of exhibits to be tendered is as follows: The 65 ter documents 3002, 3004, that is, the ICMP data documents, will be MFI'd for the time being, and then a decision will be taken later on. The rest is being admitted. Now, we have further lists. One is forthcoming from the Drago Nikolic Defence team. Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I submitted the documents. They were documents used during the cross-examination of Witness Manning, with the material that accompanied the documents that were shown in the courtroom, in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. What's the position of the Prosecution team on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any of the other Defence teams wishes to raise an objection? Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, I thought that it was my turn. I don't have any objection to the Nikolic Defence documents. I just thought that it was my turn to say something about the proposed Defence -- Popovic Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's not make it turn into an epidemic. I'll soon come to you, Ms. Tapuskovic. So there being no objection, the four Nikolic Defence team documents are being admitted. I would kindly ask the Registrar to consult with the Nikolic Defence team, whether the relevant -- whether -- in respect to items 1 and 2, whether they should be under seal or not, but it's something to be discussed amongst you. I don't know. I'm not in a position to decide on that. We finally come to you, Madam Tapuskovic. You have only got one document that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's document marked 1D449. It's a document that was shown to the witness during the cross-examination of Mr. Manning, and the witness stated his position on the document. This was a document presented to him by the Popovic Defence, and that's the only document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? Thank you, Ms. Soljan. So this document is also admitted. I know you're anxious to leave this courtroom, but there is a final matter that we wish to deal with. You will recall that recently, and also before, the Prosecution raised the issue of submitting so-called teachers edition of a portion of the duty officers log book dated from the 11th to the 23rd of July, 1995. This version of the logbook has red markings denoting the Prosecution's contentions about such matters as to the dates to which the entries pertain and the authors of the entries, and the matter was discussed comprehensively. The Nikolic, Miletic and Beara Defence teams objected to accepting the annotated logbook at this juncture as a submission, arguing that the annotations constitute arguments that should come at the close of the case rather than at this stage of the proceedings, that in addition, the Pandurevic Defence team added that the proposed submission contained mistranslations and misinterpretations. You will also recall that on the 6th of December, we further requested you to try and have negotiations and discussions amongst yourselves, and we also informed you that if no agreement was forthcoming between the parties, then we would prefer to state our position on the issue. I take it, before proceeding any further, that there has been no agreement -- no specific agreement across the board between the Prosecution and the various Defence teams, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wouldn't say there was an across-the-board disagreement. We're still talking, and the -- where we are now is that I believe the Defence were going to offer some numbers, some dates, that they didn't object to, to put up in the right-hand corner to help guide you and all of us on which dates we agreed on, and perhaps some other items, but we haven't gotten that far yet. And so we -- that's where we left it, with the understanding that they did not object to us using it, like you said, at the end of the case as a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position, Mr. McCloskey and distinguished members of the various Defence teams, is that we believe that we have given it enough time and we don't believe that there is going to be an across-the-board agreement which will be definitive and unequivocal, so we are going to tell you, in very clear terms, what our position is, and we expect you to take this into consideration and comply with our directives. Our view is that the annotations that the Prosecution referred to particularly on the 23rd of November, 2007, can serve -- can indeed serve as a valuable aid in conveying the Prosecution's contentions concerning the logbook. We are of the opinion that the submissions can be received at this stage of the case, that is indeed preferable to receive them at this stage of the case, considering that we are approaching the end of the Prosecution case. And indeed we do not believe there is any need to delay having the availability of these documents until the close of the date. It would serve no purpose. Indeed, however, we want to make it clear that the Prosecution's annotations will not be treated as evidence by the Trial Chamber. We want to put your mind at rest on that. Rather, they will be looked at as a -- simply as an aid in presenting, as I said, presenting the Prosecution's contentions, and will be solely treated as such. We also wish to make it clear that these Prosecution annotations are -- can be premised upon hearsay, as such evidence is clearly admissible before this Tribunal, according to a uniform and constant list of jurisprudence. However, as you are all aware, any hearsay statement relied upon must be in evidence before the Trial Chamber if it is to form the basis or part of the basis for an annotation, so any annotation which is based on evidence which is not before this Tribunal will, of course, be completely ignored. I hope that clears the waters and that you will understand what the position will be in relation to the document that the Prosecution wishes to make available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to note that that book is 65 ter 377A, and we will be providing you hard copies, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that disposes of another issue that we had still outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will try to make this clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Registrar has raised an important matter, issue that is more of concern to the Registrar than, really, to you or to us, because I think we have made ourselves pretty much clear. We have been asked a question, how this document is going to be treated, whether it's going to be treated as an exhibit or whether it's going to be treated as just a filing. Our position, I think, is very clear. We have already stated that it is not going to be treated as evidence. That is the starting point. So whether it's given an exhibit number or not is immaterial for us. If it is more practical for the Registrar to give it an exhibit number, then so be it. But for the real practical purpose of this document, I think the position is very clear and I think it corresponds with both the manner in which you had presented or offered this document and the way the offer was treated and considered by the various Defence teams, even those who opposed its -- it being made available. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. You will have the -- good copies of the full original of this notebook, in fact two notebooks, in the original B/C/S and in the English translation, when we finally get those done, and of course that will be the evidence, and this thing you're getting is a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for that purpose, I think it should be in the records of the proceedings, because we will, of course, consult it as we go along. We consider it as an aid, and others who may come after us may need to look at it for the same purpose as the one that justifies its availability at the time being, at the moment. So yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'd just like to clarify that the Popovic Defence team is among the teams contesting this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for pointing that out, and it will go -- it will be entered in the records, Mr. Zivanovic. We haven't finished our long journey as yet. There is still a lot to come, but at least we have in sight the end of the Prosecution case by the 1st of February. And in preparation for that and the hard work that lies ahead, I wish to take this opportunity to show the -- express the Trial Chamber's appreciation for all the good work that you have put into this case, both Prosecution and Defence, but not only Prosecution and Defence, our team, the Registrar's team, the interpreters that have such a difficult job and which many a time we perhaps are not very cooperative with - we try to do our best - the technicians, and all the others that work in the background and that we never see in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Court reporters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, court reporters. And we are going to have a recess, a well-merited one, I would say, which will serve good for everyone. We'll be able to recharge our batteries and then face the forthcoming months with greater energy. However, this recess also coincides with festive seasons. I know that there are people with -- having different religious backgrounds and denominations. It's still a festive season for everyone. For those of you who celebrate Christmas, both the one I'm used to and also the Serbian Orthodox one, Judge Prost, Judge Kwon and also Judge Stole, who couldn't be with us today, we wish to extend to you our greetings and our best wishes. We hope you will be able to enjoy Christmas with your families. And as far as the new year is concerned, of course that is a matter that we will have every reason to celebrate together. We will reconvene after the new year, and so we wish to extend again to you and to your friends and to your families our best wishes for a prosperous and fruitful new year, a new year which will see the Defence teams beginning their case and hopefully finish as well. I mean, I see some unhappy faces. But, anyway, so we leave you with this. We leave you with our best wishes. I know that almost all of you will be travelling to your places of residence, so we also wish you a safe journey to and from where you will be returning to The Hague for the January session. Thank you.
